```{r setup, include=FALSE}
m <- r$metrics[3,]

f <- r$group_metrics[1,]
male <- r$group_metrics[2,]
fn_gap <- subset(r$gaps,metric=="FNR")
fn_interval <- c(-fn_gap$upper,-fn_gap$lower)
validation_dropouts <- sum(subset(r$split_counts,split=="Validation" & target=="Dropout")$n)
validation_found <- round(r$threshold_row$Sensitivity*validation_dropouts)
```

class: title-slide

<div class="cover-copy">
<div class="kicker">STRONG TIGER &nbsp; / &nbsp; INTRODUCTION TO DATA SCIENCE</div>
<h1>Student dropout<br><span class="gradient-word">warnings.</span></h1>
<div class="cover-subtitle">How accurate are they,<br>and who gets missed?</div>
</div>
<div class="cover-bottom"><div><div class="cover-team">University of Edinburgh</div>Predictive signal. Unequal errors. A question of support.</div><div>UCI 697 &nbsp; / &nbsp; ONE PORTUGUESE INSTITUTION<br>Analysis 05 NOV 2026 &nbsp; / &nbsp; Revision 11 NOV 2026</div></div>

???
Our question is whether information known at enrolment can identify later recorded dropout, and who the same warning rule misses. We are interested in student support. We first define the outcome, then evaluate overall prediction, and finally check how errors differ between groups. We start with the label, because it determines what a warning can mean.

---
<div class="kicker">01 &nbsp; / &nbsp; DEFINE THE OUTCOME</div>

# What counts as<br>recorded dropout?

<div class="evidence-grid"><div><div class="hero-number">`r num(r$audit$rows)`</div><div class="hero-label">student records.<br>Three outcomes kept visible.</div><div class="fine-rule"></div><div class="quote-line">A course or institution change also counts as <strong>Dropout</strong>.</div></div><div>

```{r outcomes, results='asis'}
slide_plot("figures/recorded-outcomes.png","315px","Counts of Graduate, Enrolled and Dropout records at the normal course endpoint")
```

</div></div>

.small[Target: recorded dropout by the normal course endpoint.<br>Graduate and Enrolled mean no recorded dropout then. Enrolled does not mean graduated.]

.source[Realinho et al. (2022), pp. 1-4. Enrolments 2008/09-2018/19; endpoint usually 3 years, 4 for Nursing. No causal or Edinburgh-wide claim.]

???
We used `r num(r$audit$rows)` records from one Portuguese institution. We checked the original paper because dropout can mean different things. Here it includes changing course or institution, so it does not always mean leaving higher education. The outcomes were recorded at the normal end of the course, usually three years. We retained students still enrolled. In our binary analysis they have no recorded dropout at that point; they are not assumed to have graduated. These choices define what our predictions can mean.

---
<div class="kicker">02 &nbsp; / &nbsp; LOOK BEFORE MODELLING</div>

# Entry profiles overlap

```{r entry-plot, results='asis'}
slide_plot("figures/entry-profiles.png","360px","Training-set boxplots of enrolment age and admission grade by recorded outcome")
```

.takeaway[Higher median age in the recorded-dropout group.<br>Substantial overlap in admission grades. <strong>No individual outcome is determined.</strong>]

.source[Training only, n = `r num(r$configuration$training_n)`; associations, not causes.<br>Quiz 7 recommended Data to Viz; this prompted our figure review. [Boxplot advice](https://www.data-to-viz.com/caveat/boxplot.html).]

???
These plots use training records only. The dropout group had a higher median age, but ages and admission grades still overlapped. Quiz 7 pointed us to Data to Viz. Its boxplot advice reminded us to show group sizes, so we added the counts below each outcome. We kept the boxes to compare typical values and spread. These observed patterns are associations, not causes.

Figure review: Quiz 7 recommended Data to Viz. We wanted a compact comparison of the centres and spread. Its boxplot page reminded us that equal-width boxes hide group sizes, so we added the training count below each outcome. We retained boxplots for this comparison; they do not reveal the full distribution. Each panel has its own labelled units. This is our design choice, not an additional course requirement.

---
<div class="kicker">03 &nbsp; / &nbsp; A SEPARATE JOB FOR EACH DATASET</div>

# Training, validation and test

<div class="capsule-row"><div class="capsule">Age</div><div class="capsule">Admission grade</div><div class="capsule">Course</div><div class="capsule">Logistic regression → probability</div></div>

<div class="flow">
<div class="flow-card"><div class="step">01 / FIT</div><div class="flow-n">`r num(r$configuration$training_n)`</div><div class="flow-title">Training</div><div class="flow-purpose">Fit the model.</div></div>
<div class="flow-card"><div class="step">02 / CHOOSE</div><div class="flow-n violet">`r num(r$configuration$validation_n)`</div><div class="flow-title">Validation</div><div class="flow-purpose">Choose one warning threshold.</div></div>
<div class="flow-card"><div class="step">03 / EVALUATE</div><div class="flow-n accent">`r num(r$configuration$test_n)`</div><div class="flow-title">Test</div><div class="flow-purpose">Evaluate the frozen rule.</div></div>
</div>

.small[Course is categorical; age and grade are additive on the log-odds scale, without interactions.<br>Later and timing-uncertain inputs are excluded. Recorded gender is reserved for the audit.]

.learning-note[The regression lectures help us review these choices. Logistic regression required further learning.]

.source[Seed 20261105; approximately 60/20/20, stratified by original outcome and recorded gender. Model fitting and validation use no test outcomes.]

???
We use age, admission grade and course together, treating course as a category. Our model assumes additive effects on the log-odds scale, without interactions. The regression lectures help us review these assumptions; logistic regression needed further learning. We exclude later grades and financial fields with uncertain timing, and reserve recorded gender for the audit. Training records fit the model, validation records chose one threshold, and test records evaluated the frozen rule. This keeps a small model and separates its decisions. Next, we explain how probabilities become warnings.

---
<div class="kicker">04 &nbsp; / &nbsp; THE VALIDATION DECISION</div>

# Choosing the warning threshold

<div class="split-plot"><div><div class="hero-number">`r num(r$threshold,2)`</div><div class="hero-label">One common threshold.<br><br>Highest specificity while identifying at least <strong>70%</strong> of validation dropouts.<br><br>Validation sensitivity:<br><strong>`r num(validation_found)` / `r num(validation_dropouts)` = `r pct(r$threshold_row$Sensitivity)`</strong></div></div><div>

```{r threshold-plot, results='asis'}
slide_plot("figures/validation-threshold.png","385px","Validation sensitivity, specificity and warning rate across common thresholds")
```

</div></div>

.source[Our illustrative target, not a university policy. Grid 0.05-0.80 in steps of 0.01; one threshold for both groups. We then froze the rule and evaluated its sensitivity, precision and errors on test records.]

???
We wanted to find at least seventy per cent of dropout records in validation data while limiting false warnings. This illustrative target selected a common threshold of 0.31. It found 200 of 284 validation dropouts, about seventy per cent. We then froze the rule. The next slide checks test sensitivity and precision, and the cost in false warnings.

Figure review: We kept lines because the horizontal axis is a numerical threshold and the purpose is to compare how rates change. After checking Data to Viz's colour caveats, we gave all three curves different line patterns as well as colours. The curves remain descriptive validation rates, not confidence bands; the full 0-100% rate scale is retained.

---
class: tradeoff detailed-metrics

<div class="kicker">05 &nbsp; / &nbsp; OVERALL TEST PERFORMANCE</div>

# Sensitivity and precision

<div class="metric-line">
<div><div class="metric-value accent">`r pct(m$Sensitivity)`</div><div class="metric-name">Sensitivity / recall</div><div class="metric-detail">`r num(m$TP)` / `r num(m$TP+m$FN)` dropout records found</div></div>
<div><div class="metric-value violet">`r pct(m$PPV)`</div><div class="metric-name">Precision / PPV</div><div class="metric-detail">`r num(m$TP)` / `r num(m$TP+m$FP)` warnings matched</div></div>
<div><div class="metric-value">`r pct(m$Accuracy)`</div><div class="metric-name">Accuracy</div><div class="metric-detail">`r num(m$TP+m$TN)` / `r num(m$n)` decisions matched</div></div>
</div>

```{r test-table, results='asis'}
mm <- r$metrics[1:3,]
tab <- data.frame(
  Rule=c("Always no warning","Threshold 0.50",paste0("Validation rule: ",num(r$threshold,2))),
  Sensitivity=pct(mm$Sensitivity),
  `Precision (PPV)`=ifelse(is.na(mm$PPV),"Not defined",pct(mm$PPV)),
  Accuracy=pct(mm$Accuracy),check.names=FALSE)
cat(knitr::kable(tab,format="html"))
```

<div class="error-summary">0.50 to 0.31: <strong>+`r num(m$TP-default$TP)`</strong> dropout records found; <strong>+`r num(m$FP-default$FP)`</strong> false warnings. <strong>`r num(m$FN)`</strong> dropout records still missed.</div>

<div class="bridge-line">Always no warning: <strong>`r pct(r$metrics$Accuracy[1])` accuracy</strong>, but no dropouts found. Who does our rule miss?</div>

.source[Test n = `r num(m$n)`; `r num(m$FP)` false warnings; `r num(m$TP+m$FP)` / `r num(m$n)` (`r pct(m$WarningRate)`) flagged. Sensitivity 95% conditional bootstrap interval: `r interval_pct(subset(r$overall_intervals,metric=="Sensitivity")$lower,subset(r$overall_intervals,metric=="Sensitivity")$upper)`. A false warning is relative to the recorded label.]

???
Sensitivity tells us how many dropout records we find; precision tells us how many warnings match a dropout. Lowering the threshold found 107 more dropout records, but produced 177 more false warnings. Our chosen rule found 187 of 285 dropouts: about sixty-six per cent. Only 187 of its 409 warnings matched dropout: about forty-six per cent. Always giving no warning scores higher on accuracy, but finds no dropouts. That is why accuracy alone does not answer our question. We next ask who our rule misses.

---
class: fairness

<div class="kicker">06 &nbsp; / &nbsp; WHO GETS MISSED?</div>

# Who is missed by the same rule?

<div class="comparison"><div><div class="big violet">`r pct(f$FNR)`</div><div class="label">Female: `r num(f$FN)` / `r num(f$TP+f$FN)`<br>missed / dropout records</div></div><div><div class="big accent">`r pct(male$FNR)`</div><div class="label">Male: `r num(male$FN)` / `r num(male$TP+male$FN)`<br>missed / dropout records</div></div></div>

.audit-entry[Of the `r num(m$FN)` missed records, `r num(f$FN)` were female and `r num(male$FN)` male. We compare within-group rates, rather than counts alone.]

```{r fairness-plot, results='asis'}
slide_plot("figures/group-fairness.png","335px","Female circles and male triangles: five group rates with rate-specific denominators and conditional 95 percent bootstrap intervals")
```

.criterion-key[Coverage: Independence &nbsp; | &nbsp; Errors: Separation &nbsp; | &nbsp; Outcomes within warned / unwarned groups: Sufficiency]

.takeaway[False-warning rates: Female <strong>`r pct(f$FPR)`</strong>; Male <strong>`r pct(male$FPR)`</strong>.]

.small[Recorded dropout proportions: Female `r pct(f$BaseRate)`; Male `r pct(male$BaseRate)`. We investigate the differences without treating them as proof of discrimination.]

.source[Points: observed rates. n: denominator for each point. Bars: pointwise 95% percentile bootstrap intervals, conditional on the fixed model and threshold; 5,000 resamples within each group. These are not standard deviations.]

???
We focus first on missed dropouts, because a missed warning could mean a missed offer of support. The rule missed 64 of 144 female dropout records and 34 of 141 male records: forty-four versus twenty-four per cent. The gap was about twenty percentage points, with a conditional interval of roughly ten to thirty-one points. Male students had a higher false-warning rate. The other rows check who receives warnings and recorded outcomes within both prediction groups. These are independence, separation and sufficiency. Different recorded dropout rates complicate those comparisons; the gaps alone do not establish discrimination.

Figure review: We wanted to compare rates without hiding how few or how many records supported them. Data to Viz's sample-size and error-bar guidance prompted us to label each point's denominator, rather than only each group's total. We kept dots and intervals because we are comparing binary rates and their uncertainty, not the spread of a continuous variable. Circles and triangles distinguish the groups without relying on colour. We explain the interval method explicitly and use the gap intervals in backup slide 12 for direct group comparisons.

---
class: closing

<div class="kicker">07 &nbsp; / &nbsp; BEFORE REAL USE</div>

# A warning should start<br>a <span class="accent">conversation.</span>

<div class="next-grid">
<div class="next-item">Keep human review.<span>Offer support without punishment; allow records to be corrected.</span></div>
<div class="next-item">Check capacity.<span>`r pct(m$WarningRate)` flagged is a substantial support commitment.</span></div>
<div class="next-item">Investigate the errors.<span>Review both group error patterns and what the label measures.</span></div>
<div class="next-item">Test later cohorts.<span>Validate at the institution where the rule would actually be used.</span></div>
</div>

<div class="closing-statement">Predictive signal is not evidence that warnings prevent dropout.</div>

.source[One institution, historical cohorts, no cohort/year field for a chronological test. The model assumes a common additive relationship; random hold-out evaluation is not prospective validation.]

???
Our enrolment model found about two-thirds of recorded dropouts, with many false warnings and different error rates across groups. Before real use, we would check departure reasons, support capacity and performance on later cohorts at the intended institution. Any warning should lead to human review, with a way to correct records. We have not tested whether acting on warnings prevents dropout. That needs a separate evaluation of the support offered. Thank you.

---

# Backup: the three fairness questions

```{r criterion-table, results='asis'}
tab <- data.frame(
  Criterion=c("Independence","Separation","Separation","Sufficiency","Sufficiency"),
  Compare=c("Warning rate","False-positive rate","False-negative rate","Dropout among flagged (PPV)","Dropout among unflagged (1-NPV)"),
  Female=pct(c(f$WarningRate,f$FPR,f$FNR,f$PPV,f$FOR)),
  Male=pct(c(male$WarningRate,male$FPR,male$FNR,male$PPV,male$FOR)))
cat(knitr::kable(tab,format="html"))
```

.small[Recorded dropout prevalence: Female **`r pct(f$BaseRate)`**, Male **`r pct(male$BaseRate)`**. These criteria ask different questions. Equality is not assumed, and a numerical gap is not a causal finding about discrimination.]

---
# Backup: counts and denominators

```{r confusion-table, results='asis'}
tab <- data.frame(Group=c("Female","Male","Total"),
  Students=c(f$n,male$n,m$n),TP=c(f$TP,male$TP,m$TP),FP=c(f$FP,male$FP,m$FP),
  FN=c(f$FN,male$FN,m$FN),TN=c(f$TN,male$TN,m$TN))
cat(knitr::kable(tab,format="html"))
```

.small[
TP: warned and recorded Dropout. FP: warned, no recorded Dropout.<br>
FN: not warned, recorded Dropout. TN: not warned, no recorded Dropout.<br><br>
FPR = FP / (FP + TN). FNR = FN / (TP + FN).<br>
PPV = TP / (TP + FP). NPV = TN / (TN + FN).
]

# Backup: checking predicted probabilities

```{r calibration-plot, results='asis'}
slide_plot("figures/probability-calibration.png","330px","Descriptive calibration by common probability bands and recorded gender")
```

.small[We compare predicted probabilities with observed dropout proportions.<br>AUC checks ranking; Brier score checks probability error. Neither alone establishes calibration.]

.source[Colour and shape identify recorded gender; point size indicates n. Common 0.2-wide bands; n < 30 points omitted (retained in CSV). No intervals shown. This descriptive check establishes neither group calibration nor binary sufficiency.]

???
The model-checking lecture asks whether a fitted relationship describes the data adequately. For our binary outcome we examine probabilities with a calibration plot, alongside ranking and threshold errors. Points above the diagonal indicate observed dropout proportions above the average predicted risk; points below indicate lower observed proportions. Bins are coarse, small bins are omitted and no intervals are shown. This descriptive plot does not establish calibration or validate every functional-form assumption. Ordinary OLS residual-cloud rules and adjusted R-squared are not classification accuracy measures.

---
# Backup: sensitivity to the model inputs

```{r gender-sensitivity-table, results='asis'}
g <- r$gender_comparison
tab <- data.frame(
  InputSet=c("Primary: no gender","Add recorded gender"),
  AUC=num(r$metrics$AUC[c(3,4)],3),
  `Female FNR`=pct(c(f$FNR,g$FNR[1])),
  `Male FNR`=pct(c(male$FNR,g$FNR[2])),check.names=FALSE)
cat(knitr::kable(tab,format="html"))
```

Both models use the **same training rows and threshold**.<br>
The primary model was fixed before evaluating test performance.

.small[Including gender changes the error pattern; it is not an automatic fairness correction. The slight AUC improvement does not decide which allocation of errors is acceptable.]

# Backup: why keep Enrolled?

```{r enrolled-sensitivity-table, results='asis'}
tab <- data.frame(
  Analysis=c("Primary: all three labels retained","Primary fit on resolved test records","Refit excluding Enrolled"),
  TestN=num(c(m$n,r$sensitivity$n)),
  AUC=num(c(m$AUC,r$sensitivity$AUC),3),
  `Dropouts identified`=pct(c(m$Sensitivity,r$sensitivity$Sensitivity)),check.names=FALSE)
cat(knitr::kable(tab,format="html"))
```

.small[The last two rows evaluate only Dropout versus Graduate (`r num(r$sensitivity$n[1])` test records) at the same numerical threshold. They change the population and question. Better-looking numbers cannot replace the all-student endpoint analysis.]

# Backup: course connections and model assumptions

- **Course foundations:** data handling, factors, plots, bootstrap and the three fairness criteria.
- **Regression lectures:** multiple predictors, category contrasts, model checking and parsimony.
- **Fixed assumptions:** additive effects on the log-odds scale, without interactions. Interaction terms remain untested.
- **Further learning:** logistic regression, validation, thresholds, AUC and Brier score; ChatGPT and documentation.

.small[We rewrote and ran the main R analysis and checked its outputs. We now use the newer regression lectures to review those earlier choices.]

.source[Introducing linear models, pp. 48-54; Model checking and multiple linear regression, pp. 24-41, 57-63. Details: docs/course-map and docs/regression-course-update.]

???
The analysis was first evaluated on 5 November. We reviewed it against these regression lectures on 11 November. The lectures support the explanation of factor coding and multiple inputs, and help us state assumptions about interactions and complexity. They do not directly teach binomial logistic regression, and no interaction model has been fitted in this revision. Any later comparison must be developed using training and validation records, not by repeatedly selecting what looks best on the already-viewed test set.

Figure review: We wanted to compare the course mix, not ask listeners to search an alphabetical list. After reading Data to Viz's ordering advice, we sorted the six named courses by pooled training count and kept Other courses last as a combined category.
